_note: Lingo & slang reference. Same evidence discipline as the rest of this project: every entry carries a status. 'documented' means the term appears in the material this project already verifies (an episode's published summary, or a 2026 episode title/summary) and the citation is given. 'era-lexicon' means the term is real vocabulary of that period, sourced to dictionaries and scholarship, but has NOT been verified as used on screen. 'handle-with-care' means racialised or derogatory vocabulary that belongs in analysis, never in speech. 'project-jargon' means a term this site itself uses. Nothing here claims a line of dialogue.

legend.documented: Appears in the documented evidence base (episode summary or 2026 title) — citation given
legend.era-lexicon: Real vocabulary of the era, from dictionaries and scholarship — not verified as said on screen
legend.handle-with-care: Racialised or derogatory term: analysed, never spoken — see the warning on each
legend.project-jargon: A term this project uses for its own method

how_to_use: Slang is evidence, not decoration. What a text calls a thing tells you what the culture around it assumes about that thing.
Do not separate the eras by taste. 'Cuffing season' and 'going together' are two answers to the same structural question: how a relationship is named, by whom, and for how long.
The deepest layer is the oldest: signifying and the dozens are verbal traditions the 1987-1993 series actually put on screen, and the 2026 season inherits both.
Never use the handle-with-care vocabulary in your own voice, and never ask anyone to explain or perform it. It is the object of study, not the instrument.

sections.blurb: The institutional language of an HBCU campus. This is the layer the project's culture glossary only partly covers, and the season runs on it.

entries.gloss: Historically Black college or university - founded to serve Black students when most institutions excluded them. The institution the whole franchise is set in.

senses.gloss: The annual return of alumni: game, band, step show, reunions, and a campus that briefly belongs to its former students.

sections.blurb: The oldest layer, and the one worth teaching hardest: insult, praise and social control carried in the same mode. One of these was an episode's explicit subject.

entries.gloss: Indirect, artful verbal critique — insults, boasts and commentary delivered through implication, so the target must decode them.

senses.gloss: To name a person's faults in public, with accuracy as the criterion — a bad read fails and is forgotten.

senses.label: the skill sense

senses.gloss: Reading text. The course lives on this ambiguity: a text that 'reads' its characters is doing the first thing, on purpose.

senses.label: literal
senses.gloss: Shadow — the OED sense, still the primary one outside the idiom.

senses.label: the idiom
senses.gloss: Indirect disparagement: the target must work out that they were insulted. Distinguished from a direct insult precisely by the deniability.

senses.label: as a verb
senses.gloss: 'To shade someone' — to deliver it. Grammatically transitive, which is what makes it a practice rather than just a noun.

entries.gloss: Sharp, performative rebuttal — the moment a room decides the exchange has been won.
Audience completion of a speaker's line, shared by Black church practice, bands, comedy and classrooms.

senses.label: the institution
senses.gloss: Church — in Black American life a central institution of community, politics and music, and the origin of much of the register both series rely on.

senses.label: the affirmation
senses.gloss: 'Church!' as agreement: the congregation's role crossing from the sanctuary into general speech.

senses.label: the classroom
senses.gloss: A student completing the professor's line, or a room answering a performer. It is the same move in every setting, and it is why a Black classroom can sound like a call and a response at once.

entries.gloss: Moving between language varieties by context — the show's own world runs on it, from the dorm to the dean's office.

sections.title: 1987–1993 register (the original's era)
sections.blurb: Vocabulary of the original series' period. Sourced to dictionaries and scholarship — this project has not verified any of it as dialogue, because it has not watched the episodes.

entries.gloss: Stylish, attractive, well-put-together — a judgement about presentation.
New, sharp, impressive — usually about clothes or ideas.
Excellent. (Also, separately, drugs — context decides.)
An insult, or the act of insulting — direct, as opposed to signifying's indirection.
Talk that is empty or deceptive; a person full of it. Dated by the 1980s, and its presence marks a generational gap on screen.
Overreacting, or behaving absurdly.
Losing perspective, acting strangely — stronger than trippin'.
A friend from the neighbourhood or a trusted peer — a claim about origin, not just affection.
Address term among peers, kin-coded — the vocabulary of fictive kinship as much as of family.
Term of address between close male peers.
Address terms carrying political kinship as well as family meaning — 'brothers' is how the pledges' sponsors are described.
entries.evidence: S2E38 It's Greek to Me (1989-02-23) — the 'brothers' push Dwayne around

entries.gloss: Address terms that open or punctuate an exchange; gendered and generational, and central to the show's domestic register.
A one-word verdict on someone's claim — the shortest available read.
Back down, withdraw — boundary-setting in two words.
Spend time together casually — the era's word for low-stakes intimacy.
Relax; also a way of telling someone their response is disproportionate.
Departure formula.
Agreement, or a request for confirmation — 'word' can mean 'I agree' or 'for real?' depending on tone.
Emphatic agreement.
Food, or to eat.
The best — superlative praise.
Affectionate accusation: chaotic, and loved for it.
A tedious imposition.
From 'bourgeois': aspirational, status-conscious, class-policing. Whitley's whole characterisation — and the reason the show's class politics are legible at a glance.

sections.title: 2026 register (contemporary)
sections.blurb: Current vocabulary. Only 'cuffing season' is documented in this project's evidence base — and it is documented well, because the season titles an episode after it. Everything else is real contemporary language that has NOT been verified as used on screen.

entries.gloss: The cold-months scramble to pair up, named as a season with a start and an end. The 2026 season builds Episode 4 around it — and the title rewrites the original's 'those who can't teach, tutor' as 'those who can't commit, cuff'.

senses.label: the season
senses.gloss: The cold months, when pairing up is treated as a timed collective project.

senses.label: the act
senses.gloss: To cuff someone: to secure a partner before the window closes. Implies acquisition, with a hint of reluctance.

senses.label: the joke the title makes
senses.gloss: The 2026 episode title rewrites the original's 'those who can't teach, tutor' as 'those who can't commit, cuff' — the same sentence shape, a different failure.

entries.gloss: The pre-relationship phase before anyone commits to a name for it.
An ongoing intimacy with deliberately undefined status.
Introducing a partner gradually, or all at once — the relationship made visible as a curated act.
A private sexual connection kept off the public record.
Charm, specifically the ability to attract — a 2020s coinage from 'charisma'.
Self-aware delusion, usually about a relationship or an ambition.
No lie / a lie.
Quietly / openly — a way of calibrating how much a claim commits you.
Suspicious.

senses.label: the clipping
senses.gloss: Suspicious, or a suspicious person — modern clipping of 'suspect'.

senses.label: the older verb
senses.gloss: To suss (something) out: to work it out by investigation. Recorded in British and American usage long before the clipping.

entries.gloss: Undermining someone's grip on their own experience; a clinical term that became everyday vocabulary for a manipulation pattern.
This conveys… — an evaluative frame that names the vibe rather than the fact.
Emphatic full stop — the claim is closed.

senses.label: the punctuation
senses.gloss: A full stop — the ordinary mark that ends a sentence.

senses.label: the verdict
senses.gloss: In AAVE-derived usage, 'period' ends the discussion; 'periodt' intensifies it. The claim is closed and further argument is refused.

entries.gloss: Excel, especially in presentation.
Performed flawlessly.
Going to — a grammatical marker more than a word, and good evidence that the register is doing grammar, not decoration.
I swear — a truth-claim formula.
Excellent, usually of food.
Mediocre — the era's most efficient dismissal.
The felt quality of a situation, treated as information worth acting on.
'If you know, you know' — an in-group claim that also marks who is outside it.
Treating oneself as the protagonist of a scene — narration as social practice.
To lose control of oneself under pressure — a 2020s term with heavy weighting.
Agitated, or resentful — judgements about someone's emotional management.
Gossip, or the disclosing of it.
Evidence; the proof of a claim about behaviour.
Ending contact without a statement of ending — withdrawal as the message.
Sudden aversion that ends interest; feeling as verdict.
Three internet-era judgements in one row: performed correctly, occupying someone's mind uninvited, and needs to log off.
Caught with undeniable evidence — the surveillance joke as moral verdict.
Excessive, sycophantic praise.
'Be f***ing for real' — a demand that someone stop pretending.
Overreacting, by consensus of the room.

sections.title: Handle with care — racialised and derogatory vocabulary
sections.blurb: These are terms found in the era's media, in Black media criticism, and in the scholarly literature about how Black people have been described. They belong in analysis with their history attached, never in the instructor's mouth, and no student should be asked to explain or perform them. One of them was the explicit subject of a 1991 episode.

entries.gloss: The racialised stereotype of the devoted Black domestic servant — the imagery a 1991 episode put at the centre of a campus exhibit, precisely to argue about it.
entries.evidence: S5E105 Mammy Dearest (1991-12-05) — Whitley stages an exhibit on images of Black women; a fellow student objects to the Mammy artefacts

entries.gloss: A gendered insult for a woman, comparing her to livestock; dated, and heavy even in its own period.
Class-and-gender slurs aimed at Black women, coded by class and neighbourhood. Their use tells you who the speaker thinks they are.
A racialised political figure invented to make poverty a character flaw and state support a scandal — one of the era's most effective pieces of political language.
A framing phrase that turns a documented set of economic conditions into a claim about character; the subject of the 1965 report the course studies.
A racial slur with an in-group reclamation whose rules are strict, contested and not the instructor's to test.
A term of class contempt that does geographic and racial work — 'that's ghetto' is always an argument about who is properly middle class.
A controlling image that converts a legitimate grievance into a character defect, and disciplines the person voicing it.

sections.title: This project's own jargon
sections.blurb: Terms the sites and the course use for their own method. A reader meeting them for the first time should not have to infer them.

entries.gloss: A 2026 element that returns to something in the 1987–1993 series — a title, a character, an institution, a storyline.
A callback carried in the episode's name, where the rewrite is the joke: 'Reconcilable Differences' becomes 'Irreconcilable Differences'.
The kind of callback: lore (an institution or place), theme (an idea or storyline), cast (a returning actor or character), or title echo.
How well evidenced a claim is. 'Verified' means traceable to a published record; 'interpretation' means it is a reading that could be argued with.
Documented (a checkable fact), interpretation (a reading of what a text argues) and hypothesis (a claim put up for testing). The course grades on keeping them apart.
The franchise's habit of putting a serious social crisis in the fifth or seventh slot of a season — HIV in 1991, an unnamed crisis in 2026.
This site's shorthand for the returning women of the original cast, who arrive in 2026 as a generation with authority.
The revival's structure: the leads are the children of the original's leads, so the show is about inheritance before it is about anything else.
Both premieres aired on 24 September — 1987 and 2026.
A single documented callback entry on this site, with its scene, its origin and its sources.
